title: Maps and Navigation (Google Maps)
summary: Design a mapping service with tile rendering, route planning, ETAs, and live traffic.
statement: Design a maps and navigation service. Clients display map tiles at many zoom levels, search addresses, request routes with ETAs, and receive turn-by-turn guidance that accounts for live traffic. Start by clarifying requirements and estimating scale, then design the system and defend your decisions.
initialGuidance: Clarify the users, the main journeys, and what is explicitly out of scope before drawing anything.
Estimate read and write volume and storage growth; the numbers decide which components you need.
Name the guarantees you will offer (consistency, durability, availability) and the trade-offs behind them.
Write down assumptions as you make them and revisit them when requirements change.
coreFunctionalRequirements: Serve map tiles at multiple zoom levels.

requirementQuestions.question: How many users, tile requests, and route requests per second?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Sets read and write rates and storage growth, which decide whether a single node can cope.

requirementQuestions.question: How fast must tiles load and routes compute?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Defines which paths need caching, precomputation, or regional placement.

requirementQuestions.question: How big is the road graph and how often does map data change?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Determines the data model, retention, and storage choices.

requirementQuestions.question: Which travel modes, offline maps, and live traffic?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Fixes what is in and out of the design so effort goes to what matters.

requirementQuestions.question: Can navigation continue offline if connectivity drops?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Determines redundancy and failover design, and which features may degrade instead of failing.

requirementQuestions.question: How is tile delivery cost controlled?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Prevents over-engineering and affects build-versus-buy choices.

workloadAssumptions.illustrativeNote: All numbers below are illustrative examples for practice and are not benchmarks. Real answers depend on the requirements the candidate negotiates.

estimationPrompts: How many tiles exist across zoom levels and how much storage do they need?
How much memory does a regional routing graph need?
How many probe data points per second feed traffic?

keyDecisions.question: How are tiles delivered?
considerations: Pre-rendered raster or vector tiles served from object storage via CDN.
Cache and long TTLs; regenerate on data change.

keyDecisions.question: How are routes computed fast?
considerations: Contraction hierarchies or similar preprocessing on the road graph.

keyDecisions.question: How is traffic incorporated?
considerations: Aggregate anonymised location probes into edge speeds.

keyDecisions.question: How are addresses resolved?
considerations: Index of addresses and places with fuzzy matching.

keyDecisions.question: How is re-routing handled?
considerations: Client sends position updates; server checks deviation.

tradeoffs.tension: Fast static queries versus dynamic edge weights.
Better routes versus distraction and load.

commonMistakes: Running Dijkstra on the whole planet graph per request.
Rendering tiles on demand without caching.
Treating traffic data as exact and fresh.
followUps: How do you support offline maps?
How do you compute ETAs for a future departure time?
How do you update the map for road closures quickly?
How do you protect user location privacy in probe data?
